title: How AI Applications Earn Their Premium | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z partner argues AI application companies keep a pricing premium only if they out-execute customers' build-or-prompt alternatives, make proprietary context cheaper to rent than rebuild, and prove value with task-level pricing. Cites Harvey/Repsol, Decagon/Notion, Clay, and an August 2026 survey where 94% of enterprise LLM buyers expect higher spend.

themes.theme: Pricing power erosion from model progress

insights.claim: Cheaper inference can lift application margins, but more capable models and easier development tools also make parts of an application easier to replace, so the commercial question is what customers keep paying for as alternatives improve.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Margin tailwind from falling inference costs is offset by commoditization risk to app-layer premiums.

insights.claim: An application is vulnerable when a customer can reproduce its core output with a general-purpose model and little ongoing effort; exposure varies by product.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Screen AI app holdings by how reproducible the core output is with a frontier model.

insights.claim: Pricing is especially important now but is often overlooked or postponed because fast-growing AI companies are reluctant to tackle it.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Under-developed pricing is a latent weakness in high-growth AI app companies.

insights.claim: Model progress continually improves the customer's alternative, so an application's advantage must widen faster than that alternative improves for the premium to persist.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Premium durability depends on a widening, not static, moat.

insights.claim: The buy test is whether the application offers a better combination of total cost, quality, speed, and risk than the customer's best credible alternative, including implementation, operation, and maintenance effort.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete build-vs-buy diligence lens.

themes.theme: Rule 1: operate the workflow better than the customer

insights.claim: Customers do not need to rebuild a whole application to weaken pricing power; moving one high-volume task in-house or establishing a credible alternative can be enough to challenge the premium.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Partial insourcing is the main threat to vendor pricing.

insights.claim: A buyer at a global professional-services firm said that if a direct prompt to a frontier model beat a vendor's productivity tool, it saw little reason to pay the platform premium; the firm built an internal AI platform able to run models locally or on premises and was experimenting with open-source alternatives.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Large enterprises are building credible internal alternatives, capping thin-wrapper pricing.

insights.claim: In contract review, defensibility means applying a company's legal standards, keeping edits consistent across a document, and preserving context as negotiations evolve.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Specialized workflow depth is what justifies paying over raw models.

insights.claim: Harvey's Playbook Review uses a lead agent distributing review to specialized agents, reconciling conflicting edits and checking the finished document, with models chosen per task by quality, speed, and cost and review context preserved for follow-ups.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Multi-agent orchestration with per-task model routing is the template for app-layer execution moats.

insights.claim: Learning from which redlines lawyers accept, edit, or reject could let future reviews need less guidance, so an application's advantage can compound with use.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Usage-driven feedback loops are a candidate data moat for vertical AI apps.

insights.claim: In a blind evaluation by Repsol's legal team, Harvey beat Microsoft Copilot and the internal prototype Lexia on quality, then on accuracy and time savings in an eight-week pilot with 50 lawyers across 12 jurisdictions; Harvey reports 4-6 hours saved per lawyer per week and 96% adoption across the legal department.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Vendor-reported but shows a specialized app winning a head-to-head against big-tech and in-house builds.

themes.theme: Rule 2: context cheaper to rent than rebuild

insights.claim: Context justifies a premium through exclusive access, useful preparation, or both; private observations customers cannot obtain elsewhere have standalone value, while accessible information is valued by the cost of making it accurate, current, and usable.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Separates durable proprietary data moats from preparation services that are easier to replicate.

insights.claim: A vertical software company with years of proprietary pricing benchmarks on roughly 3,000 companies was exploring exposing them through an MCP server so AI systems can query them directly.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Proprietary datasets monetized via MCP is an emerging distribution model for incumbents.

insights.claim: Vendors earn margin on context by collecting, validating, and maintaining it once and spreading the cost across many customers, so each customer rents reliable context for less than rebuilding it.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Economies of scale in data upkeep underpin context-as-a-service pricing.

insights.claim: Even customer-owned data such as policies, CRM records, contracts, and workflow history requires permissions, normalization, retrieval, and ongoing validation to be usable, and an application can earn its fee by doing that work.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Integration and data-prep labor is a fee-justifying layer even without proprietary data.

themes.theme: Rule 3: prove value, then price to capture it

insights.claim: In an August 2026 survey of 100 enterprise LLM decision-makers, 94% expected total LLM spending to increase and 37% expected it to at least double in the next year.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Rising enterprise LLM budgets bring scrutiny of ROI, favoring vendors with measurable value.

insights.claim: Applications should measure the full delivery cost per recognizable unit of work (retrieval, model calls, tools, retries, evaluation, human review), including failed attempts, to get cost per successfully completed unit.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Unit economics per successful task is the right margin metric for AI apps.

insights.claim: Decagon's Notion case reports up to a 34% improvement in ticket resolution time; Notion considered building internally but chose an external solution to focus on its core platform.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Example of a buyer choosing buy over build for support automation.

insights.claim: Applications should price at the highest layer of value they can reliably measure, attribute, and defend, and should not price per token; credits are a currency, not a value metric, and should map to tasks or intuitive effort levels.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Outcome or task-based pricing is favored over token pass-through for AI apps.
insights.quote: Credits are a currency, not a value metric

insights.claim: Clay found fixed AI prices overcharged simple workloads and made complex ones unprofitable, so it separated Data Credits from Actions for orchestration, kept fixed credits for bounded AI workloads, and passed through actual token costs with no markup for variable reasoning models.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Hybrid pricing separating predictable work from volatile model cost is an emerging pattern.

insights.claim: Tying price to recognizable work lets a vendor use routing, caching, or better models to improve margins, cut prices, or include more work as delivery costs fall, without customers tracking model mix.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten
insights.so_what: Task-based pricing lets vendors retain cost-deflation gains while sharing some with customers.
